The paper develops a coupled set of three integral equations to solve for tangential electric and magnetic fields on the cavity aperture and surface.
The integral equations are based on fundamental electromagnetic field laws rather than surface or volume equivalence principles.
The unknown tangential fields have finite support limited to the cavity aperture and surface.
A moment-method algorithm specialized for axisymmetric cavities is used for numerical solution.
Unknown fields are expanded using piecewise-linear functions in elevation and complex exponentials in azimuth.
Orthogonality of complex exponentials reduces the size of the moment method matrix.
The numerical solution is well-conditioned and uniquely solvable at frequencies where other methods have spurious solutions.
Open cavities embedded in UAV wings can enhance RCS without increasing aerodynamic drag or weight significantly.
An electrically controllable membrane covering the aperture can switch the OCRED on or off.
Physical models of spherical, deep cylindrical, conical, and shallow cylindrical OCREDs were fabricated and measured.
Experimental RCS measurements agree well with numerical predictions, validating the model.
Open cavities scatter strongly over large bandwidths, broad aspect angles, and arbitrary polarizations.
Traditional high-frequency asymptotic methods (PO, PTD, GO, UTD) do not accurately predict OCRED scattering.
The cavity interior is filled with a homogeneous, isotropic, linear dielectric material.
The ground plane and cavity walls are assumed perfectly conducting in the canonical problem.
The study addresses the resonance regime where cavity dimensions are on the order of a wavelength.
RCS enhancement is important for UAV tracking, decoys, stealth aircraft camouflage, and target identification.
The integral equation approach avoids modeling equivalent currents on the infinite ground plane.
The moment-method matrix condition number and Fourier mode importance are analyzed for different geometries.
The dissertation includes both theoretical development and experimental validation.
The aperture rim edge condition is satisfied by the numerical solution.
The study fills a gap in open literature on experimental data for open cavity scattering.
The OCRED concept allows in-flight switching of RCS enhancement.
The dissertation was completed in March 1997 at the Air Force Institute of Technology.
